First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Age: 21 years

Sex: Male

Complaint: Three-day history of progressively worsening right scrotal pain, accompanied by gradual swelling of the right hemiscrotum. Pain has increased to the point of discomfort with walking; acetaminophen provided no relief.

Analysis: The clinical presentation is most consistent with acute epididymitis (epididymo-orchitis). Supporting findings include subacute onset of unilateral scrotal pain and swelling, tenderness over the right epididymis and testis on palpation, and Doppler ultrasonography demonstrating significantly increased vascularity of the right testicle and epididymis with a small reactive hydrocele. The patient is a sexually active young man with multiple partners and no condom use, making sexually transmitted pathogens — most commonly Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae — the most likely etiology. The most critical differential diagnosis, testicular torsion, is effectively excluded by the preserved bilateral cremasteric reflexes and the Doppler finding of increased (rather than absent or decreased) blood flow. Other considerations such as torsion of the appendix testis, testicular tumor, trauma, and inguinal hernia are less likely given the normal testicular echogenicity, absence of a mass, lack of trauma history, and the imaging findings. No red flags for sepsis or necrotizing infection are present: the patient is afebrile, normotensive, has a normal heart rate, appears nontoxic, and has no abdominal tenderness, skin changes, or crepitus.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: First-catch urine nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (STD panel, currently pending); urine culture (currently pending). No additional imaging is required given the diagnostic Doppler ultrasound findings.

Conclusion: The patient has acute epididymitis, most likely of sexually transmitted origin, with testicular torsion effectively ruled out by clinical examination and Doppler ultrasonography. He is clinically stable, afebrile, and without signs of systemic infection or complications, and can be managed safely on an outpatient basis.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Urology

Recommendations: Initiate empiric antimicrobial therapy covering both N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis — ceftriaxone (single intramuscular dose) plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10–14 days — pending STD panel results. Provide supportive measures including scrotal elevation and support, rest, and analgesics (e.g., NSAIDs), as acetaminophen was ineffective. Arrange close follow-up with reassessment in 48–72 hours to confirm symptom improvement; if there is no improvement or worsening, re-evaluate for complications such as abscess formation or alternative diagnoses, with urology referral if indicated. Educate the patient on safe sex practices and condom use, and arrange partner notification and treatment for all recent sexual contacts to prevent reinfection and further transmission. Offer HIV testing and consider screening for syphilis and hepatitis given the high-risk sexual history. Ensure reportable disease notification if gonorrhea is confirmed.

Sex: Female

Complaint: A 62-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of gnawing epigastric pain that is worse on an empty stomach and partially relieved by eating, accompanied by early satiety and occasional nausea. She has a 3-year history of daily naproxen use for osteoarthritis and consumes one glass of wine nightly. She denies vomiting, hematemesis, melena, or unintentional weight loss.

Analysis: The clinical picture is most consistent with NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease, likely a duodenal ulcer, given the classic pattern of pain worsened by fasting and relieved by food, in the setting of chronic daily naproxen use. Early satiety and nausea are compatible with gastroduodenal mucosal injury. The patient is hemodynamically stable with normal vital signs, no peritoneal signs (no rebound or guarding), a negative fecal occult blood test, and only mildly reduced hemoglobin (12.1 g/dL), which together indicate no acute hemorrhage or perforation and support a non-emergent pathway. Age over 60 with new-onset dyspepsia and early satiety is an alarm feature that warrants endoscopic evaluation to exclude malignancy, although the absence of weight loss, vomiting, and overt bleeding lowers that probability. Main differential considerations include NSAID-induced gastritis, gastric or duodenal ulcer, Helicobacter pylori-associated ulcer disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease, functional dyspepsia, and less likely gastric malignancy or biliary tract disease. Daily alcohol intake may act as a synergistic mucosal irritant alongside the NSAID.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with gastric biopsies for histology and Helicobacter pylori testing; non-invasive H. pylori testing (urea breath test or stool antigen) if endoscopy is deferred.

Conclusion: The presentation is most consistent with NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease (likely duodenal ulcer) in a stable patient without red-flag features of acute bleeding or perforation. Age over 60 and early satiety warrant endoscopic evaluation to confirm the diagnosis and exclude malignancy, with H. pylori testing as an essential component of management.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology

Recommendations: Discontinue or reduce naproxen if possible, and initiate a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) such as omeprazole to promote mucosal healing and symptom relief. Arrange outpatient upper endoscopy (EGD) with biopsies for H. pylori and histology, given age over 60 and persistent dyspepsia. Test for and treat H. pylori if present, as co-infection increases ulcer risk and eradication reduces recurrence. Counsel the patient on moderating nightly alcohol consumption, as it may contribute to mucosal irritation in combination with NSAIDs. Advise the patient to seek urgent care if she develops vomiting, hematemesis, melena, severe abdominal pain, or worsening anemia. Consider alternative analgesia for osteoarthritis if naproxen is discontinued.

winner_protocol:
Age: 34
Sex: Male
Complaint: Left ankle pain, swelling, and inability to bear weight after an inversion injury sustained while stepping off a curb, with a reported audible crack at the time of injury.
Analysis: The patient presents with an acute inversion injury of the left ankle. The mechanism, inability to bear weight, significant swelling and ecchymosis over the lateral malleolus, point tenderness over the distal fibula, and palpable bony tenderness at the posterior edge of the lateral malleolus are consistent with a lateral malleolus fracture. Ankle radiographs confirm a non-displaced transverse fracture of the distal fibula (Weber B) with no talar shift. The medial malleolus is nontender, and neurovascular status is intact, indicating no immediate limb-threatening compromise. The main differential considerations include lateral ankle ligament sprain (ATFL/CFL tear), syndesmotic (high ankle) sprain, medial malleolus fracture, talar dome osteochondral injury, fifth metatarsal base avulsion fracture, and Maisonneuve fracture (proximal fibula fracture). Although static radiographs show no talar shift, syndesmotic instability or occult deltoid ligament disruption cannot be fully excluded, and the anterior drawer test was unreliable due to pain and guarding.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Standard ankle radiographs have already been obtained and are adequate for initial diagnosis. Additional studies needed include stress or weight-bearing radiographs to assess syndesmotic stability, and a proximal fibula radiograph or physical examination to rule out a Maisonneuve fracture. CT or MRI may be indicated at orthopedic follow-up if syndesmotic instability or a talar dome osteochondral lesion is suspected.
Conclusion: This is a non-displaced Weber B distal fibula (lateral malleolus) fracture without talar shift in a 34-year-old man with intact neurovascular status. The injury is stable on static imaging but requires timely orthopedic evaluation to exclude occult syndesmotic or medial-sided instability that could convert it to an unstable bimalleolar-equivalent injury.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Orthopedics
Recommendations: Immobilize the left ankle in a well-padded posterior splint or rigid walking boot (avoid early circumferential casting due to swelling and risk of fracture blisters). Instruct the patient to remain non-weight-bearing with crutches, and to use ice, elevation, and oral analgesia for symptom control. Refer the patient to orthopedics within 1–2 weeks for repeat examination and imaging (including stress or weight-bearing views) to confirm stability and determine whether operative or continued non-operative management is needed. Perform a physical exam of the proximal fibula to exclude a Maisonneuve fracture and assess the fifth metatarsal base for tenderness. Reassess the anterior drawer test and ATFL integrity after pain subsides. Counsel the patient on signs of compartment syndrome (increasing pain, pallor, paresthesias, pulselessness) despite currently intact neurovascular status. Assess VTE risk given lower extremity immobilization and reduced mobility, and consider DVT prophylaxis as appropriate. Consider MRI at follow-up if pain persists after fracture healing to evaluate for talar dome osteochondral lesions.

winner_protocol:
Age: 40
Sex: Male
Complaint: Difficulty falling and staying asleep for the past 5 nights, with daytime fatigue and difficulty concentrating, in the context of a recent major work project with a tight deadline and associated anxiety.
Analysis: The patient presents with acute, short-term insomnia (5 nights) that is temporally linked to an identifiable situational stressor (work deadline) and is likely exacerbated by ongoing caffeine consumption until mid-afternoon. He reports only 4–5 hours of sleep per night with daytime fatigue and concentration difficulties, but denies depressed mood, anhedonia, or suicidal ideation, and has no prior history of sleep disorders. Examination is notable only for mild fatigue; vital signs, neurological exam, and mental status exam are unremarkable. The clinical picture is most consistent with acute insomnia secondary to situational stress, with caffeine use as a contributing factor. Differential considerations include adjustment disorder with anxiety, generalized anxiety disorder, other primary sleep disorders (e.g., obstructive sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome), and medical or substance-induced causes of sleep disturbance; however, the acute onset, clear stressor, and normal examination make these less likely at this time. No urgent medical or psychiatric pathology is suggested.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: This is an acute, short-term insomnia episode driven by situational work-related stress and caffeine intake, without evidence of major depressive disorder, other psychiatric illness, or underlying medical or primary sleep disorder. The condition is appropriate for self-care with supportive management and monitoring; no emergent or urgent intervention is indicated.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Psychiatry
Recommendations: 
- Advise sleep hygiene measures: consistent sleep/wake schedule, a quiet and dark sleep environment, and avoidance of stimulating activities near bedtime.
- Recommend restricting caffeine intake, specifically discontinuing coffee after early afternoon, given the patient's current consumption until mid-afternoon.
- Suggest stimulus control techniques (e.g., using the bed only for sleep, getting up if unable to fall asleep within ~20 minutes) and relaxation or stress management strategies (e.g., brief mindfulness, controlled breathing) to address the work-related anxiety.
- Counsel on monitoring functional impairment and safety, particularly regarding driving and work performance, given daytime fatigue and concentration difficulties.
- Advise follow-up if symptoms persist beyond 2–4 weeks or worsen; reassess for other sleep disorders (e.g., sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome) and medical causes if the insomnia becomes chronic.
- Consider referral to a mental health professional if anxiety severity increases, depressive symptoms emerge, or functional impairment becomes significant; short-term pharmacotherapy may be discussed only if non-pharmacologic measures fail and symptoms persist.
Notes: The patient's caffeine use and situational stress are the primary modifiable contributors; if insomnia persists beyond a few weeks despite these measures, further evaluation for primary sleep disorders or psychiatric conditions is warranted. No red-flag symptoms (e.g., mood disturbance, suicidal ideation, abnormal exam) are present.

Vignette:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the clinic by her parents for a spreading rash around her mouth and nose that began 5 days ago. It started as a small red spot near her left nostril and has since developed into multiple crusty lesions. Several children at her daycare have had similar sores. She is otherwise well with no fever, sore throat, or decreased appetite. On examination, there are multiple well-defined erosions with thick golden-yellow (honey-colored) crusts clustered around the nares and upper lip, with two satellite lesions on the left cheek. The lesions range from 1 to 3 cm in size. There is no warmth, fluctuance, or deep tissue involvement. There is mild left submandibular lymphadenopathy. The remainder of the skin examination is normal. She has no history of eczema or immunodeficiency.
winner_protocol:
Age: 5 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Spreading rash around the mouth and nose, beginning as a small red spot near the left nostril 5 days prior, now with multiple crusty lesions; several daycare contacts have similar sores.
Analysis: The presentation of multiple well-defined erosions with thick golden-yellow (honey-colored) crusts clustered around the nares and upper lip, with satellite lesions on the left cheek, in a systemically well child with daycare exposure, is classic for non-bullous impetigo (impetigo contagiosa). The most likely causative pathogens are Staphylococcus aureus and/or Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus). The absence of fever, sore throat, decreased appetite, warmth, fluctuance, or deep tissue involvement supports a superficial, localized, and benign process. Mild left submandibular lymphadenopathy is consistent with regional reactive changes and does not indicate deep infection. Differential considerations include herpes simplex virus infection, allergic/irritant contact dermatitis, tinea faciei, bullous impetigo, early cellulitis/erysipelas, and secondary bacterial infection of minor trauma or insect bites; these are less likely given the characteristic morphology and distribution. No red flags such as high fever, systemic toxicity, rapidly spreading erythema, significant warmth, tenderness, skin peeling, or fluctuance are present.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. Diagnosis is clinical; routine bacterial cultures and wound swabs are not indicated at the initial evaluation. Cultures are reserved for atypical, recurrent, or treatment-resistant cases, or suspected MRSA.
Conclusion: This 5-year-old girl has non-bullous impetigo (impetigo contagiosa), a superficial bacterial skin infection most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus and/or Streptococcus pyogenes. The condition is localized, non-emergent, and appropriately managed in an outpatient pediatric primary care setting. Prognosis is excellent with appropriate topical therapy and infection-control measures.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations: 
- Initiate topical antibacterial therapy for the localized lesions, such as mupirocin 2% ointment or retapamulin, applied 2–3 times daily for 5–7 days. Gently remove crusts with warm water and soap before application.
- Reserve oral antibiotics (e.g., agents covering Group A Streptococcus and, if indicated, MRSA) for extensive disease, systemic involvement, or failure to respond to topical therapy within 3–5 days.
- Emphasize strict hand hygiene and avoidance of sharing towels, linens, or other fomites; keep fingernails short to reduce autoinoculation and spread.
- Provide daycare exclusion guidance: exclude the child until 24–48 hours after starting antibiotics or until lesions are healed/dried, to prevent transmission to contacts.
- Counsel parents to monitor for treatment failure within 3–5 days and to return for reassessment if lesions worsen, spread, or new systemic symptoms (fever, pain, spreading erythema, fluctuance) develop.
- Monitor for post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) in the weeks following infection; advise parents to watch for hematuria (cola-colored urine), periorbital edema, oliguria, or hypertension and seek evaluation if these occur.
- Consider MRSA risk, especially if lesions are purulent, recurrent, or refractory; obtain culture and adjust antibiotics accordingly in such cases.
- In recurrent cases, consider intranasal S. aureus carriage and decolonization with intranasal mupirocin.
- Treat symptomatic daycare contacts as appropriate and reinforce infection-control measures in the daycare setting.
Notes: Underlying skin barrier disruption (e.g., minor trauma or insect bites) may serve as the portal of entry. The absence of eczema or immunodeficiency reduces the risk of complicated infection. Bullous impetigo remains a differential but is less likely given the honey-colored crusts; however, it can occasionally coexist or evolve. If lesions fail to respond to topical therapy, oral antibiotics covering MRSA and Group A Streptococcus may be required.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Chest X-ray to rule out structural pathology, pneumonia, mass, or pneumothorax, particularly given the history of uterine cancer; fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO) to confirm eosinophilic airway inflammation; allergy testing given the clear environmental trigger; spirometry with pre- and post-bronchodilator assessment (already performed and diagnostic).
Conclusion: This is a 47-year-old woman with new-onset cough-variant asthma / reactive airway disease triggered by secondhand tobacco smoke exposure, complicated by secondary costochondritis. The diagnosis is supported by reversible airflow obstruction on pulmonary function testing and the temporal relationship to an environmental irritant. The patient is clinically stable, well-appearing, and without red flags, making outpatient management appropriate.

Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology

Vignette:
An 8-year-old girl is brought to the pediatrician by her mother for intense itching that has been worsening over the past 2 weeks. The itching is particularly severe at night and disrupts her sleep. Her mother reports that her younger brother and father have recently developed similar itching. On examination, there are numerous small erythematous papules and excoriations in the interdigital web spaces of both hands, the flexor surfaces of the wrists, the axillary folds, and the periumbilical area. winner_protocol:
Age: 8 years

Sex: Female

Complaint: Intense, progressive pruritus over the past 2 weeks, worse at night and disrupting sleep, with similar itching recently developing in the younger brother and father. Examination shows numerous small erythematous papules and excoriations in the interdigital web spaces of both hands, flexor surfaces of the wrists, axillary folds, and periumbilical area, with several short linear burrows (5–10 mm) in the finger web spaces. Face and scalp are spared; no vesicles or bullae are present.

Analysis: The clinical presentation is classic for scabies, an infestation by Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis. Strong supporting facts include the characteristic distribution (interdigital web spaces, flexor wrists, axillary folds, periumbilical area) with sparing of the face and scalp, the presence of pathognomonic linear burrows, intense nocturnal pruritus, and the positive family history (brother and father with similar symptoms), indicating household transmission. Definitive confirmation is provided by the mineral oil preparation from a burrow scraping, which demonstrated mites, eggs, and fecal pellets under microscopy — the diagnostic gold standard. Main differential considerations include atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, papular urticaria/insect bites, impetigo, and dyshidrotic eczema, all of which can present with pruritic papules but are distinguished by the absence of burrows and the negative microscopic findings. The absence of vesicles or bullae helps exclude bullous disorders such as bullous pemphigoid or dermatitis herpetiformis. The condition is uncomfortable and highly transmissible but not life-threatening, warranting timely non-emergent outpatient management.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None — the diagnosis is already confirmed by the mineral oil preparation microscopy of a burrow scraping, which revealed mites, eggs, and fecal pellets. No further diagnostic testing is needed.

Conclusion: This is an uncomplicated case of scabies in an 8-year-old girl, confirmed by microscopic identification of Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis mites, eggs, and fecal pellets. The clinical picture, including nocturnal pruritus, characteristic burrows and papular excoriations in typical locations, and affected household contacts, supports the diagnosis. The condition requires non-emergent care and is appropriately managed in the pediatric/primary care setting.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics

Recommendations:
- Treat the patient with first-line topical permethrin 5% cream applied from the neck down, left on for 8–14 hours, then washed off; repeat the application in 7–14 days.
- Treat all household and close contacts simultaneously, even if asymptomatic, to prevent reinfestation.
- Perform environmental decontamination: wash bedding, towels, and clothing used in the preceding 3–4 days in hot water and dry on high heat; seal non-washable items in plastic bags for at least 72 hours.
- Counsel the family that post-scabetic pruritus may persist for 2–4 weeks after successful treatment due to host hypersensitivity; manage symptomatically with oral antihistamines or mild topical corticosteroids.
- Re-evaluate clinically in 2–4 weeks to confirm resolution and detect treatment failure, reinfestation, or complications.
- Monitor for secondary bacterial infection (impetigo, cellulitis) at excoriation sites; initiate antibiotics if signs of superinfection develop, and be aware of the risk of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis if secondary streptococcal pyoderma occurs.
- Assess household contacts for special populations (pregnant, lactating, infants <2 months) when selecting a scabicide (e.g., permethrin vs. sulfur), and evaluate immunocompromised contacts for possible crusted (Norwegian) scabies, which would require more aggressive treatment.
- Inquire about the potential source of infestation (school, daycare, close contacts) to prevent re-exposure.
- Assess the impact of sleep disruption on the child's school performance and daily functioning.
- Note that oral ivermectin is an alternative if topical treatment fails or is impractical, but it is not first-line in young children.

Notes:
- In older children and adults, the face and scalp are typically spared, as in this case; however, in infants, the face, scalp, palms, and soles may be involved.
- The positive family history underscores the need for family-wide treatment to eradicate the infestation.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Vignette:
A 49-yr-old woman comes to the emergency department because of chest pain. She says she
was in her usual state of health until the day before, when she awoke at 6 am with the sudden
onset of sharp left-sided chest pain. Pain has been constant and radiates to the center of her
chest. It is not worsened by exertion, movement, food, activity, or respiration. She also had
shortness of breath and chills but no cough, nausea, or diaphoresis. She took 400 mg of
naproxen without relief. The pain has persisted, prompting her to come to the emergency
department now. She has never had chest pain before this episode and has no known history of
cardiac or pulmonary disease.

Review of Systems:
General: Chills as noted in History of Present Illness. She thought she had a fever but did not
take her temperature.

Skin: Noncontributory

HEENT: No recent URI symptoms.

Pulmonary: As per History of Present Illness.

Cardiovascular: Chest pain as per History of Present Illness. No palpitations or syncope. She
has noted dyspnea with climbing stairs since chest pain began; dyspnea resolves quickly with
rest and is not worsened by lying flat.

Gastrointestinal: No abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting. Appetite and bowel movements are
normal.

Genitourinary: Minimal spotting after recent menses.

Musculoskeletal: She has no current musculoskeletal symptoms, although she has noted
intermittent left leg swelling and discomfort for the past year. There is no history of injury or

recent immobilization. The last time she had swelling and discomfort in her left leg was about 10
days ago.

Neurologic: Noncontributory

Psychiatric: Noncontributory

Past Medical History:
Medical history: Menorrhagia due to uterine fibroids, with secondary iron-deficiency anemia;
endometriosis; right breast fibroadenoma. No history of blood clots or clotting disorder.

Surgical history: Laparoscopy and lysis of adhesions for endometriosis; tubal ligation; excision
of breast fibroadenoma.

Medications: None

Allergies: None

Family history: Mother was recently diagnosed with stage IV colon carcinoma; brother has
schizophrenia.

Social history: No tobacco or alcohol use; former cocaine and heroin use (quit both more than
20 yr ago); works for the hospital in the food services department. No recent travel.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Appears anxious and in some pain. No cyanosis or respiratory distress.

Vital signs:
Temperature 36.8° C
Pulse 107 beats/min
BP right arm 130/72 mm Hg
Respirations: 16/min
O2 saturation 96% on room air

Skin: No lesions or rashes.

HEENT: Mucus membranes moist, no oral lesions, patent nares.

Pulmonary: Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. No crackles or wheezes.

Cardiovascular: Elevated rate, regular rhythm. No murmurs, rubs, or gallops. No tenderness to
palpation. No jugular venous distention. Normal carotid pulse.

Gastrointestinal: bdomen nontender and nondistended with normal bowel sounds.

Genitourinary: Uterus palpated just below the umbilicus. No blood in vaginal vault.

Musculoskeletal: No joint deformity, full range of motion without pain. Lower extremities: no
swelling, erythema, or tenderness.

Neurologic: Cranial nerves intact; muscle strength and sensation intact throughout.

Mental status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and time.

Test Results:
Results of appropriate laboratory testing return and show:
Serum D-dimer level: 395 ng/mL [2.16 nmol/L]
Hemoglobin: 9.7 g/dL
Platelets: 330,000/mcL
WBC: 10,600/mcL
Serum troponin I level: 0.05 ng/mL [0.05 mcg/L]

ECG is obtained and is shown.

CT scan of the chest with IV contrast is obtained and shows a filling defect in bilateral upper and
lower segmental pulmonary arteries on pulmonary arterial phase.

Age: 49 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Sudden onset of sharp left-sided chest pain radiating to the center of the chest, constant and not worsened by exertion, movement, food, activity, or respiration; associated with shortness of breath and chills, without cough, nausea, or diaphoresis. Pain persisted despite 400 mg naproxen, prompting emergency department presentation.
Analysis: The patient presents with acute chest pain, dyspnea, and tachycardia (pulse 107 beats/min). The CT scan of the chest with IV contrast demonstrates filling defects in bilateral upper and lower segmental pulmonary arteries on the pulmonary arterial phase, which is diagnostic of acute bilateral pulmonary embolism. Supporting clinical features include a history of intermittent left leg swelling and discomfort over the past year (with the last episode approximately 10 days ago), suggesting an underlying deep vein thrombosis as a potential embolic source; an enlarged uterus palpated below the umbilicus (consistent with uterine fibroids) that may cause pelvic venous compression and stasis; and an elevated D-dimer level (395 ng/mL). The mildly elevated troponin I level (0.05 ng/mL) and tachycardia raise concern for right ventricular strain (intermediate-risk/submassive PE). The patient is hemodynamically stable (BP 130/72 mm Hg, O2 saturation 96% on room air), with no evidence of shock or respiratory distress. Main differential considerations prior to confirmatory imaging included acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, tension pneumothorax, acute pericarditis/myopericarditis, pneumonia/pleuritis, and musculoskeletal chest pain; however, the CT findings definitively confirm pulmonary embolism and effectively rule out these alternatives. The patient's anemia (hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL) is consistent with her known menorrhagia from uterine fibroids.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Transthoracic echocardiography to assess for right ventricular strain/dysfunction; lower extremity (and pelvic) venous Doppler ultrasound to evaluate for residual deep vein thrombosis or extrinsic venous compression; serial troponin measurements; electrocardiogram (already obtained); continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring. Additional evaluation for an underlying hypercoagulable state or occult malignancy may be considered given the family history of stage IV colon carcinoma and recurrent leg swelling.
Conclusion: Acute bilateral segmental pulmonary embolism in a hemodynamically stable but tachycardic 49-year-old woman with a mildly elevated troponin, concerning for intermediate-risk (submassive) PE with possible right ventricular strain. The clinical picture, supported by definitive CT angiography, requires urgent risk stratification and immediate therapeutic anticoagulation.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Initiate immediate therapeutic-dose anticoagulation (e.g., low-molecular-weight heparin, unfractionated heparin, or a direct oral anticoagulant) unless contraindicated. Perform transthoracic echocardiography to assess right ventricular size and function, and obtain serial troponin levels to further risk-stratify. Obtain lower extremity venous Doppler ultrasound to identify residual deep vein thrombosis. Admit the patient to a monitored inpatient setting for ongoing observation and management. Assess hemodynamic stability to determine whether thrombolysis is indicated; given current stability, anticoagulation alone is the appropriate initial approach. Evaluate for an underlying hypercoagulable state or occult malignancy, particularly given the family history of colon carcinoma and the recurrent left leg swelling. Address the patient's iron-deficiency anemia and menorrhagia in the context of uterine fibroids as part of ongoing care.
Notes: The D-dimer value (395 ng/mL) is near the normal threshold and does not exclude pulmonary embolism when clinical suspicion is high and definitive CT angiography confirms bilateral emboli. Physical examination for deep vein thrombosis has low sensitivity, and the absence of leg swelling on exam does not exclude a venous source. The patient is hemodynamically stable, but PE can deteriorate rapidly; close monitoring is essential.

Age: 72
Sex: Male
Complaint: Two days of worsening confusion, fever, and decreased oral intake in a 72-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia and recent urinary tract infection; now obtunded, hypotensive, and febrile with a distended bladder.
Analysis: The patient presents with septic shock secondary to urosepsis / complicated urinary tract infection with acute urinary retention. Strongest supporting facts include fever (T 39.4°C), hypotension (BP 76/44, MAP 55 mmHg), hyperlactatemia (5.8 mmol/L), obtundation, acute kidney injury (creatinine 3.2 mg/dL from baseline 1.2), thrombocytopenia (82,000/mcL), marked leukocytosis with left shift (WBC 24,800/mcL, 22% bands), procalcitonin 48 ng/mL, and SOFA score of 11. Urinalysis showing too numerous to count WBC and bacteria, suprapubic tenderness, and 800 mL of cloudy, foul-smelling urine on catheterization confirm a urinary source with obstruction/retention. Main differential considerations include complicated pyelonephritis, prostatic abscess, emphysematous cystitis/pyelonephritis, resistant bacterial infection (e.g., ESBL), and septic encephalopathy versus an acute structural intracranial event; other sepsis sources (pneumonia, abdominal) and non-infectious causes of shock (cardiogenic, hypovolemic) should also be excluded, though the urinary source is strongly suggested.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Renal and bladder ultrasound (or non-contrast CT abdomen/pelvis) to evaluate for hydronephrosis, perinephric abscess, or prostatic abscess; repeat serial lactate; arterial blood gas; coagulation panel (given thrombocytopenia); consideration of lumbar puncture if meningitis remains a concern. Blood and urine cultures have already been obtained.
Conclusion: This is septic shock from urosepsis with multi-organ dysfunction (SOFA 11), driven by a complicated urinary tract infection with acute urinary retention due to BPH. The patient requires immediate, aggressive resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, source control via bladder decompression, and intensive care; delayed intervention carries high short-term mortality.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Emergency
Recommendations: Continue broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering resistant uropathogens; aggressive IV crystalloid resuscitation targeting MAP ≥ 65 mmHg and lactate clearance; initiate vasopressor support (e.g., norepinephrine) if MAP remains < 65 mmHg despite fluids; maintain Foley catheter drainage as source control, with urology consultation for possible persistent obstruction, prostatic abscess, or need for further drainage; admit to ICU for close monitoring. Repeat serial lactate, coagulation panel, and blood gas to assess resuscitation response and evaluate for DIC. Obtain renal/bladder ultrasound or non-contrast CT to rule out obstructive uropathy or abscess requiring intervention. Target endpoints include MAP ≥ 65 mmHg, lactate normalization, adequate urine output (>0.5 mL/kg/h), improvement in mental status, and stabilization of vital signs. Address the consideration of septic encephalopathy versus structural intracranial event if mental status does not improve with resuscitation.

A 38-year-old man is brought in by ambulance after sudden onset of severe vertigo, diplopia, and difficulty swallowing while at work 90 minutes ago. He has no significant past medical history and takes no medications. On examination, he is alert but dysarthric. Vital signs: T 37.0C, HR 78, RR 16, BP 168/94, SpO2 98%. Neurological exam reveals left-sided Horner syndrome, right-sided limb ataxia, decreased pain and temperature sensation on the left face and right body, and absent gag reflex on the left. winner_protocol:
Age: 38
Sex: Male
Complaint: Sudden onset of severe vertigo, diplopia, and difficulty swallowing while at work 90 minutes prior to presentation, accompanied by dysarthria.
Analysis: The patient presents with an acute posterior circulation ischemic stroke, specifically a left lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, confirmed by CT angiography showing left vertebral artery occlusion. The clinical findings are classic and localize precisely to the left lateral medulla: left-sided Horner syndrome (descending sympathetic fibers), decreased pain and temperature sensation on the left face (spinal trigeminal tract) and right body (spinothalamic tract), right-sided limb ataxia (inferior cerebellar peduncle), and absent left gag reflex with dysphagia and dysarthria (nucleus ambiguus). The CT head is negative for hemorrhage, ruling out hemorrhagic stroke. The main differential considerations include other posterior circulation strokes (cerebellar or brainstem infarcts), brainstem hemorrhage, vestibular neuritis, and migraine with brainstem aura; however, the CTA-confirmed left vertebral artery occlusion strongly supports ischemic stroke. In a 38-year-old with no prior medical history, vertebral artery dissection is the most important etiology to consider, followed by cardioembolism or a hypercoagulable state. The case is time-critical: symptom onset was 90 minutes ago, NIHSS is 12, and a large vessel occlusion is present, placing the patient well within the therapeutic window for acute reperfusion therapy.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI brain with DWI and MRA to confirm and delineate the extent of the acute infarct; echocardiogram and cardiac monitoring to evaluate for cardioembolic source; laboratory studies including lipid profile and HbA1c for secondary prevention workup; continuous monitoring of respiratory status and airway protective reflexes.
Conclusion: Acute left lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome due to left vertebral artery occlusion, presenting as a hyperacute ischemic stroke with large vessel occlusion. The patient requires emergent neurological and neurointerventional evaluation for time-sensitive reperfusion therapy, with careful attention to airway protection given brainstem involvement.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Neurology
Recommendations: Activate the acute stroke team immediately. Evaluate the patient for intravenous thrombolysis (e.g., tenecteplase or alteplase) given presentation within the 4.5-hour window, non-hemorrhagic CT, and disabling deficits (NIHSS 12), provided no contraindications exist. Urgently evaluate for endovascular mechanical thrombectomy given the confirmed left vertebral artery large vessel occlusion and significant neurological deficits. Prioritize airway protection: the patient has severe dysphagia, dysarthria, and an absent left gag reflex, posing high risk for aspiration and respiratory compromise; maintain NPO status and prepare for possible intubation. Manage blood pressure per acute stroke guidelines. Admit to a stroke unit with continuous cardiac and respiratory monitoring. Investigate the etiology, with particular attention to vertebral artery dissection in this young patient, and initiate appropriate secondary prevention once reperfusion decisions are made.
Notes: Brainstem involvement carries a high risk of respiratory failure, aspiration pneumonia, and progression of stroke; malignant edema and cardiac arrhythmias are additional potential complications. MRI with DWI is more sensitive than CT for acute posterior circulation infarcts and should be obtained to confirm the exact extent of the medullary lesion.

- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. winner_protocol:
Age: 68 years

Sex: Male

Complaint: A 68-year-old man with known mild heart failure presents with a 1-week history of progressive dyspnea on exertion (now stopping every few steps), bilateral lower extremity edema, 2-pillow orthopnea, cough with white phlegm, wheezing, and a 3-kg weight gain. He denies chest pain, palpitations, syncope, or fever. Despite reported medication compliance and dietary adherence, symptoms have worsened, and prior outpatient furosemide dose increases were ineffective.

Analysis: The clinical picture is that of acute decompensated heart failure with systemic congestion (JVD 12 cm, bibasilar crackles, bilateral pleural effusions, edema to the thighs, hepatomegaly, orthopnea, 3-kg weight gain) occurring in the setting of a restrictive cardiomyopathy. The echocardiogram shows preserved LVEF (55%) with severe concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, restrictive diastolic filling (E/A > 2, low tissue Doppler velocities), and biatrial enlargement — a pattern classic for infiltrative cardiac amyloidosis. The fat pad biopsy is diagnostic of systemic amyloidosis (Congo red-positive with apple-green birefringence). The combination of MGUS, macroglossia, and cardiac-dominant phenotype strongly favors light-chain (AL) amyloidosis, though transthyretin (ATTR, wild-type or hereditary) and secondary (AA, given rheumatoid arthritis) must be excluded by tissue typing. The low blood pressure (92/64 mm Hg), prior syncope, orthostatic dizziness, and erectile dysfunction suggest autonomic dysfunction and possible conduction system involvement. Markedly elevated BNP (1420 pg/mL) with mildly elevated troponin indicates advanced cardiac involvement and carries prognostic significance. The patient is at high risk for hemodynamic deterioration given hypotension, preload dependence of the stiff ventricle, and progressive congestion refractory to outpatient diuretics. Differential considerations before biopsy confirmation included hypertensive heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, constrictive pericarditis (excluded by lack of pericardial thickening and normal inspiratory flow variation), sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, and Fabry disease; the biopsy result confirms amyloidosis.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (SPEP/UPEP with IFE); serum free light chain (FLC) assay; mass spectrometry-based proteomic typing of the fat pad biopsy tissue; bone marrow biopsy; cardiac MRI; 99mTc-PYP scintigraphy; TTR genetic sequencing; 24-hour urine for proteinuria and renal function assessment; serial troponin and BNP monitoring; ambulatory rhythm monitoring or electrophysiology evaluation given prior syncope and conduction risk; screening for sleep-disordered breathing given macroglossia.

Conclusion: This patient has systemic amyloidosis with cardiac involvement, most likely AL type given the MGUS and macroglossia, presenting as acute decompensated heart failure with restrictive cardiomyopathy, severe congestion, and borderline hypotension. He requires urgent hospitalization for hemodynamic stabilization, careful diuresis, definitive amyloid subtyping, and coordinated multidisciplinary management.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Cardiology

Recommendations:
1. Admit urgently for inpatient management of acute decompensated heart failure with continuous hemodynamic and renal monitoring. Initiate cautious IV diuresis (e.g., furosemide) with careful titration to avoid over-diuresis, given preload dependence and low baseline blood pressure; consider invasive hemodynamic monitoring if deterioration occurs.
2. Avoid beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, as these can precipitate severe hypotension in cardiac amyloidosis. Digoxin is contraindicated due to binding to amyloid fibrils and heightened toxicity risk.
3. Obtain definitive amyloid subtyping urgently via serum free light chains, serum and urine immunofixation, and mass spectrometry-based proteomic typing of the biopsy tissue; do not assume AL from clinical context alone. Perform bone marrow biopsy to characterize the plasma cell clone. Consider TTR genetic testing and 99mTc-PYP scintigraphy to exclude ATTR.
4. Refer to cardiology with subspecialty expertise in heart failure/amyloidosis as primary, with concurrent hematology/oncology consultation for clone-directed therapy (e.g., bortezomib-based regimen with daratumumab/dexamethasone for AL; tafamidis if ATTR is confirmed). Referral to a multidisciplinary amyloidosis center is ideal.
5. Evaluate for conduction system disease given prior syncope and orthostatic dizziness; consider ambulatory rhythm monitoring or electrophysiology consultation for possible pacemaker placement.
6. Manage warfarin carefully given atrial fibrillation and potential acquired factor X deficiency or hepatic involvement; monitor INR closely and adjust if invasive procedures are planned.
7. Assess for autonomic dysfunction (orthostatic vitals, erectile dysfunction history) and screen for sleep-disordered breathing given macroglossia.
8. Monitor serial troponin and BNP as staging and prognostic biomarkers; watch for signs of hemodynamic collapse or arrhythmia during diuresis.

Notes: The mildly elevated troponin (0.03 ng/mL) likely reflects chronic myocardial injury from amyloid infiltration rather than acute coronary syndrome, but serial monitoring is warranted. Low voltage on ECG (voltage-to-mass discordance) is a hallmark clue for cardiac amyloidosis and should be correlated with the echo findings. The history of rheumatoid arthritis raises the possibility of AA amyloidosis, though the cardiac-dominant phenotype and MGUS make AL far more likely; tissue typing is mandatory. Prognosis depends on amyloid type (AL worse than ATTR), stage, and response to disease-modifying therapy, so early diagnosis and typing are critical.

Vignette:
A 50-year-old obese man with a BMI of 34 presents with a 6-month history of persistent heartburn and acid regurgitation despite taking omeprazole 20 mg daily. He reports the heartburn is worse after large meals and when lying down, and he frequently wakes at night with a sour taste in his mouth and occasional coughing. He has tried elevating the head of his bed and avoiding late meals with only partial relief. He denies dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, or hematemesis. He drinks two to three beers on weekends and does not smoke. On examination, vital signs are normal. He is an obese man in no acute distress. Abdominal exam reveals mild epigastric tenderness. There is no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. His dentist has noted enamel erosion on posterior teeth.
winner_protocol:
Age: 50
Sex: Male
Complaint: 6-month history of persistent heartburn and acid regurgitation despite omeprazole 20 mg daily, worse after large meals and when lying down, with nocturnal sour taste in the mouth, occasional coughing, and posterior dental enamel erosion noted by the dentist.
Analysis: The patient presents with classic symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) that are refractory to standard once-daily proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy. Strong supporting facts include persistent heartburn and regurgitation exacerbated by large meals and recumbency, nocturnal symptoms with sour taste and cough, obesity (BMI 34) as a major risk factor, and posterior dental enamel erosion indicating proximal reflux. The absence of alarm features (dysphagia, odynophagia, weight loss, hematemesis) and stable vital signs with a chronic 6-month course support non-emergent care. The main differential considerations for refractory symptoms include erosive esophagitis, Barrett's esophagus, non-erosive reflux disease (NERD), functional heartburn, eosinophilic esophagitis, peptic ulcer disease, hiatal hernia, and esophageal motility disorders (e.g., achalasia). Cardiac disease was mentioned as a less likely consideration given the chronic pattern but was not emphasized by the panel.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD / upper endoscopy) to evaluate for erosive esophagitis, Barrett's esophagus, hiatal hernia, or alternative pathology. If EGD is normal, ambulatory esophageal pH-impedance monitoring and esophageal manometry may be needed to differentiate acid reflux, non-acid reflux, and functional disorders.
Conclusion: This is refractory GERD with extraesophageal manifestations (nocturnal cough, dental enamel erosion) in an obese 50-year-old male, partially responsive to once-daily omeprazole. The patient is clinically stable with no red flags, and the condition warrants timely outpatient gastroenterology evaluation with upper endoscopy to assess mucosal damage and exclude complications such as Barrett's esophagus.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology
Recommendations: 1) Optimize PPI therapy: ensure proper timing (30-60 minutes before breakfast), assess adherence, and consider increasing to twice-daily dosing or switching agents before labeling as truly refractory. 2) Reinforce lifestyle modifications: weight loss (targeting BMI reduction), avoid large and late meals, elevate the head of the bed, and minimize alcohol intake. 3) Perform EGD to evaluate for erosive esophagitis, Barrett's esophagus, hiatal hernia, and other upper GI pathology; test for Helicobacter pylori if gastritis or ulceration is found. 4) Refer to dentistry for protective measures against enamel erosion. 5) Screen for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) given obesity and prominent nocturnal reflux. 6) Inquire about over-the-counter NSAID use, which could contribute to epigastric tenderness and ulcer risk. 7) If EGD is normal, consider ambulatory pH-impedance monitoring and esophageal manometry to clarify the reflux phenotype. 8) If anti-reflux surgery is contemplated later, obtain esophageal manometry first to rule out motility disorders.
Notes: This patient is at high risk for Barrett's esophagus and esophageal adenocarcinoma based on demographic risk factors (male, age ≥50, chronic GERD, obesity), so endoscopic surveillance considerations apply. Cardiac disease was raised by one expert as a less likely differential but was not emphasized by the panel.

winner_protocol:
Age: 28 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Pain on the palmar surface of the left index finger after accidentally touching a hot pan approximately 1 hour prior; the finger was immediately cooled under running water.
Analysis: The patient presents with a clear history of acute thermal contact injury to a single digit. Examination shows diffuse erythema of the palmar left index finger from the fingertip to the proximal interphalangeal joint, with intact skin, no blistering or blanching, tenderness to light touch, warmth, capillary refill under 2 seconds, and preserved sensation and range of motion. These findings are consistent with a superficial (first-degree) thermal burn limited to the epidermis. The absence of blistering, skin breakdown, neurovascular compromise, or functional impairment rules out partial-thickness or full-thickness injury. Differential considerations include contact dermatitis, allergic reaction, friction injury, early cellulitis, or delayed blistering indicating a superficial partial-thickness burn, but the clear thermal mechanism and acute presentation make superficial burn the most likely diagnosis. No red flags are present.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: This is a superficial (first-degree) thermal burn of the palmar left index finger. winner_protocol:
Age: 20
Sex: Female
Complaint: Bilateral itchy, watery eyes for the past 3 days, with onset shortly after spring pollen counts increased; associated bilateral conjunctival injection and mild chemosis with clear watery discharge. No eye pain, photophobia, purulent discharge, or vision changes.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for uncomplicated seasonal allergic conjunctivitis. Supporting facts include the temporal correlation with elevated spring pollen counts, a known history of seasonal allergies, bilateral ocular pruritus with watery discharge, conjunctival injection, mild chemosis, intact visual acuity, and the absence of preauricular lymphadenopathy. The diagnosis is clinical. Main differential considerations include viral conjunctivitis (typically unilateral with preauricular lymphadenopathy and foreign body sensation), bacterial conjunctivitis (purulent discharge and eyelid matting), dry eye syndrome (burning/foreign body sensation without prominent seasonal pruritus), and toxic/irritant or contact lens-related conjunctivitis. These are excluded by the classic history and physical findings. No red flags (eye pain, photophobia, reduced visual acuity, purulent discharge, pupil abnormalities, preauricular lymphadenopathy) are present, and no urgent referral is indicated.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None. No laboratory, imaging, or culture studies are indicated; the diagnosis is entirely clinical.
Conclusion: This is a mild, uncomplicated case of seasonal allergic conjunctivitis in a 20-year-old female with a known history of seasonal allergies. The condition is self-limited and appropriate for self-care with over-the-counter measures. No urgent or emergent intervention is required, and the patient can be managed conservatively with monitoring for red flags and non-emergent re-evaluation if symptoms persist.
Emergency type: Self-care appropriate
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology
Recommendations: 
- Initiate conservative management: strict allergen avoidance (e.g., staying indoors during high pollen counts, closing windows, using air conditioning), cool compresses applied to closed eyelids, and frequent use of preservative-free artificial tears.
- Use over-the-counter topical dual-action antihistamine/mast cell stabilizer eye drops (e.g., ketotifen or olopatadine) as first-line pharmacotherapy. Avoid topical vasoconstrictor eye drops due to the risk of rebound conjunctival hyperemia (medication overuse conjunctivitis) with prolonged use.
- Advise against eye rubbing to prevent corneal abrasion and further mast cell degranulation.
- Assess contact lens wearing status; if the patient wears contact lenses, evaluate for microbial keratitis or giant papillary conjunctivitis, and consider contact lens-related conjunctivitis. Advise discontinuation of lens wear until symptoms resolve if applicable.
- Assess for associated allergic rhinitis or asthma; if present, consider systemic antihistamines or intranasal corticosteroids.
- Educate on proper eye drop administration technique (e.g., avoiding touching the dropper tip to the eye, waiting between different drops).
- Do not initiate topical corticosteroids without specialist monitoring due to risks of elevated intraocular pressure, cataract formation, and exacerbation of herpes simplex keratitis.
- Re-evaluate on a non-emergent basis if symptoms do not improve after 48–72 hours of appropriate therapy, or immediately if red flags develop (vision loss, severe eye pain, photophobia, or purulent discharge), which would warrant urgent ophthalmologic evaluation.
- Consider referral for allergen immunotherapy in cases of severe or recurrent symptoms, and advise starting prophylactic treatment before the next pollen season.
Notes: If the patient has a history of asthma or atopic dermatitis, she may be at higher risk for more severe or persistent allergic eye disease, such as vernal or atopic keratoconjunctivitis, and should be monitored accordingly. Although the consensus is self-care appropriate, a non-emergent evaluation may be reasonable if symptoms persist or prescription options are needed.

criterion:

criterion:

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:

Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.

It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Age: 26

Sex: Female

Complaint: 3-day history of sharp, steady lower abdominal pain radiating bilaterally across the lower abdomen, with new-onset nausea and vomiting, inability to tolerate oral intake, fever, chills, urinary frequency, and incomplete bladder emptying in an 18-week pregnant patient.

Analysis: The patient presents with a classic constellation of findings for acute pyelonephritis in pregnancy. Strongest supporting facts include high fever (38.8°C), marked tachycardia (120 bpm), bilateral costovertebral angle tenderness, leukocytosis (WBC 17.0 x 10³/µL), and a urinalysis showing positive leukocyte esterase, positive nitrites, numerous bacteria, and 30–50 WBCs per high-power field. The 18-week gestation is a significant risk factor for upper urinary tract infection due to pregnancy-related urinary stasis and ureteral dilation. The patient's vomiting, dry mucous membranes, urine ketones, and mildly elevated BUN (23 mg/dL) indicate significant dehydration and risk of ketosis. The fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis raise concern for systemic inflammatory response syndrome and possible early sepsis. Main differential considerations include acute cystitis, acute appendicitis, chorioamnionitis, nephrolithiasis, ovarian torsion, gastroenteritis, and ectopic pregnancy (less likely at 18 weeks). However, the bilateral CVA tenderness, fever, and definitive urinalysis findings strongly favor pyelonephritis. The absence of hydronephrosis on renal ultrasound does not exclude pyelonephritis. The bilateral CVA tenderness is somewhat atypical and warrants consideration of bilateral stones or papillary necrosis if clinical improvement is delayed. Faint left basal inspiratory crackles require monitoring for endotoxin-mediated acute lung injury/ARDS or fluid overload during resuscitation.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urine culture with antimicrobial susceptibility testing (obtained before starting antibiotics); blood cultures; serum lactate to assess for sepsis; complete blood count with differential; renal function tests; fetal heart rate monitoring (non-stress test or biophysical profile); uterine activity monitoring for preterm contractions; repeat renal ultrasound or CT imaging for nephrolithiasis if symptoms persist despite therapy.

Conclusion: This is acute pyelonephritis in an 18-week pregnant patient with systemic signs of infection, dehydration, and inability to tolerate oral intake. The condition requires emergent hospital admission for intravenous hydration, pregnancy-safe intravenous antibiotics, antiemetics, and close maternal-fetal monitoring due to high risks of sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome, preterm labor, and fetal distress.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Obstetrics and Gynecology

Recommendations: Admit the patient to the hospital for inpatient management. Initiate aggressive intravenous hydration to correct dehydration and ketosis. Start empiric broad-spectrum pregnancy-safe intravenous antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone, or ampicillin plus gentamicin, or cefepime); avoid fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines. Administer parenteral antiemetics and antipyretics. Obtain urine culture and blood cultures before starting antibiotics to guide definitive therapy. Monitor maternal vital signs closely for progression to sepsis or septic shock, including serum lactate. Perform regular fetal heart rate auscultation/monitoring and uterine activity monitoring for preterm contractions. Monitor maternal respiratory status closely given faint left basal crackles, with vigilance for ARDS or fluid overload during resuscitation. Monitor renal function during IV hydration given the mildly elevated BUN. If clinical improvement is delayed, consider imaging for nephrolithiasis (CT or repeat ultrasound) given bilateral CVA tenderness and absence of hydronephrosis on initial ultrasound. After acute treatment, initiate daily suppressive antibiotic prophylaxis for the remainder of the pregnancy due to high recurrence rates. Note that if beta-agonist tocolytics are needed for preterm labor, they may exacerbate the patient's mild asthma; use with caution. Group B Streptococcus status is not specified; recurrent UTIs with GBS may influence intrapartum management and should be addressed.

Notes: The absence of hydronephrosis on renal ultrasound does not exclude pyelonephritis. Bilateral CVA tenderness is atypical; consider bilateral stones or papillary necrosis if no improvement. Positive blood on urinalysis may reflect hematuria from infection or nephrolithiasis. Scant thin white cervical discharge with closed os and no cervical motion tenderness makes cervicitis/PID less likely, but closed os does not fully exclude chorioamnionitis if membranes were ruptured. The patient's tachycardia and fever may indicate early sepsis, requiring prompt intervention.

Vignette: A 10-year-old girl is brought in by her parents who report she frequently feels nauseated and dizzy during car rides, particularly on winding roads. Symptoms have been occurring for the past year and typically resolve within 15 to 20 minutes after stopping the vehicle. She does not vomit. Sitting in the front seat and looking out the window helps somewhat. She denies hearing loss, tinnitus, headaches, or similar symptoms outside of car rides. On examination, she is well-appearing and in no distress. Vital signs are age-appropriate. Neurological exam, including cranial nerves and cerebellar testing, is normal. Otoscopic exam is unremarkable.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.
case_text:
Vignette:
A 10-year-old girl is brought in by her parents who report she frequently feels nauseated and dizzy during car rides, particularly on winding roads. Symptoms have been occurring for the past year and typically resolve within 15 to 20 minutes after stopping the vehicle. She does not vomit. Sitting in the front seat and looking out the window helps somewhat. She denies hearing loss, tinnitus, headaches, or similar symptoms outside of car rides. On examination, she is well-appearing and in no distress. Vital signs are age-appropriate. Neurological exam, including cranial nerves and cerebellar testing, is normal. Otoscopic exam is unremarkable.
winner_protocol:
Age: 10 years
Sex: Female
Complaint: Frequent nausea and dizziness during car rides, particularly on winding roads, occurring over the past year and resolving within 15–20 minutes after stopping the vehicle. No vomiting. Symptoms are partially relieved by sitting in the front seat and looking out the window. No hearing loss, tinnitus, headaches, or symptoms outside of car rides.
Analysis: The presentation is classic for motion sickness (kinetosis). The strongest supporting facts are the strict temporal relationship between passive vehicular motion and symptom onset, rapid resolution upon stopping the vehicle, partial relief with visual-vestibular realignment (front seat, horizon gazing), and a completely normal physical, otoscopic, and neurological examination. The mechanism involves a mismatch between vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive inputs. The absence of vomiting is not atypical, as nausea can occur without vomiting. Relevant differential considerations include vestibular migraine, benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood, labyrinthitis, central posterior fossa lesions, and anxiety-related dizziness; these are unlikely given the absence of headaches, auditory symptoms, spontaneous episodes outside car rides, and neurological abnormalities. No red flags are present.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None
Conclusion: This 10-year-old girl has benign, self-limited motion sickness (kinetosis) with no evidence of underlying otologic, vestibular, or central nervous system pathology. The condition warrants non-emergent primary pediatric care for confirmation, education, and management guidance.
Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics
Recommendations:
- Reassure the parents that motion sickness is a common, benign childhood condition with a peak incidence between ages 2 and 12 years, and that it often improves with age.
- Advise non-pharmacological first-line measures: sitting in the front seat (if age/weight appropriate), focusing visual gaze on the external horizon, ensuring adequate cool ventilation/fresh air, taking breaks during long trips, and avoiding reading or screen use while in transit.
- If symptoms interfere with daily activities (e.g., school trips, family vacations), consider prophylactic use of an age-appropriate first-generation antihistamine (e.g., dimenhydrinate or diphenhydramine) taken 30–60 minutes prior to travel.
- Avoid transdermal scopolamine in younger children due to a higher risk of adverse central and anticholinergic side effects.
- Document any prior trials of over-the-counter motion sickness medications and their efficacy or side effects.
- Inquire about activities that exacerbate symptoms during the ride (e.g., reading, electronic device use) and about family history of motion sickness or migraine, as these may be relevant predisposing factors.
- Assess the impact of symptoms on daily activities to guide the aggressiveness of pharmacological management.
- Provide clear return precautions: seek reevaluation if symptoms occur outside car rides, worsen, or are accompanied by new neurological signs such as morning vomiting, persistent headaches, progressive ataxia, hearing loss, persistent vertigo outside of motion, or focal neurological deficits.
- Note that children with significant motion sickness have an increased risk of developing migraines later in childhood or adolescence; keep this in mind during future follow-up.
Notes: None

criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.

The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol

Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.
